title: Dichotomy for finite-domain restricted CSPs
formal:
Assume \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\). For every finite relational signature \(\tau\), every finite \(\tau\)-structure \(A\), and every possibly infinite \(\tau\)-structure \(B\) for which \(\operatorname{CSP}(B)\) is decidable, must \(\operatorname{RCSP}(A,B)\) be either polynomial-time solvable or NP-hard in the source’s completion sense? Explicitly, let
\[\mathcal S_{A,B}=\{S\subseteq\{0,1\}^*:S\text{ is decidable and }S\cap\operatorname{CSP}(B)=\operatorname{CSP}(A)\cap\operatorname{CSP}(B)\}.\]
Is it always true that
\[\bigl(\exists S\in\mathcal S_{A,B}:S\in\mathrm P\bigr)\quad\lor\quad\bigl(\forall S\in\mathcal S_{A,B}:S\text{ is NP-hard}\bigr)?\]
The input is a finite structure \(X\) promised to map homomorphically to \(B\); on that promise the decision is whether \(X\) maps to \(A\).
why: This asks whether the finite-domain CSP dichotomy survives every decidable restriction described by homomorphisms into a fixed, possibly infinite structure. A positive answer would sharply constrain the complexity introduced by such promises. A counterexample would demonstrate intermediate promise behaviour even though all satisfying assignments still use a fixed finite domain.

importance.reason: The question tests how far the finite-domain CSP dichotomy survives decidable infinite input promises and whether homomorphism-defined restrictions can produce intermediate complexity.
importance.basis: Individual reading of the source’s promise semantics, finite-restriction theorem and exact open-question quantifiers.

sentences: A restricted CSP asks whether a finite input maps to a fixed finite target, under the promise that it maps to another fixed structure.
The restriction structure may be infinite, but the source requires its finite-input CSP to be decidable.
The question asks whether every such promise problem is polynomial-time solvable or NP-hard when P differs from NP.
Hardness must hold for every decidable completion of the promised answers, and the known dichotomy only covers finite restrictions.
A resolution would determine whether decidable homomorphism promises preserve the finite-domain dichotomy or allow intermediate behaviour.

definitions:
A finite relational signature \(\tau\) is a finite list of relation symbols of positive integer arities. A \(\tau\)-structure \(D\) has a domain and a relation \(R^D\subseteq D^r\) for each \(r\)-ary symbol. The target \(A\) is finite; the restriction \(B\) may have an arbitrary infinite domain. A homomorphism \(h:D\to E\) is a function preserving every relation tuple: \((d_1,\ldots,d_r)\in R^D\) implies \((h(d_1),\ldots,h(d_r))\in R^E\). Write \(D\to E\) for existence of such a map. Maps need not be injective. Neither \(A\to B\) nor \(B\to A\) is assumed.

Input structures have domain \([n]\), \(n\geq0\), and explicitly listed tuples for each relation. Encode \(n\) in unary, then the relation lists in signature order with unary list lengths and binary coordinate indices. Let \(L\) be the total bit length. Empty relations, repeated coordinates and isolated elements are allowed; repeated listed tuples are harmless. Define \(\operatorname{CSP}(D)\) as the set of valid encodings of finite \(X\) with \(X\to D\). Invalid encodings do not belong to this set. Empty template domains may be included; their trivial boundary cases do not alter the question.

For each problem \(A,B,\tau\) are fixed, and only \(X\) is supplied. An input in \(\operatorname{CSP}(B)\) must be accepted exactly when it lies in \(\operatorname{CSP}(A)\); outside the promise either answer is allowed. A completion \(S\) is a total decidable language with precisely this behaviour on the promise. Since \(A\) is finite, \(\operatorname{CSP}(A)\) is a decidable completion, so \(\mathcal S_{A,B}\) is never empty. Decidability of \(\operatorname{CSP}(B)\) is a hypothesis recovered from the source, not a polynomial-time promise-recognition assumption. No description, relation-table algorithm, homomorphism into \(B\), or oracle for \(B\) is supplied. Infinite restrictions are not limited to finitely presented or categorically specified structures.

A completion is in \(\mathrm P\) if a deterministic multitape Turing machine accepts exactly it and halts on every string of length \(L\) within \(C(L+1)^k\) bit steps for fixed positive integers \(C,k\). The machine and constants may depend on \(A,B\). Decidable means a deterministic machine halts and decides membership, without any time bound. No uniform procedure for constructing these machines from templates, common polynomial exponent, advice or randomness is requested.

A language is in \(\mathrm{NP}\) if membership has polynomially bounded certificates checkable in deterministic polynomial time. A language \(S\) is NP-hard here under deterministic polynomial-time many-one reductions: for every \(K\in\mathrm{NP}\), there is a total polynomial-time function \(f_K\) with \(x\in K\) if and only if \(f_K(x)\in S\). Equivalently, it suffices to reduce Boolean three-clause satisfiability, where each clause has at most three literals. This is hardness of the total language \(S\), not a claim that \(S\) itself lies in NP.

The promise-hardness quantifiers are \(\forall\text{ decidable completions }S\ \exists\text{ suitable reductions to }S\). Reductions may depend on \(S\); no single reduction whose images always satisfy \(X\to B\) is required by this definition. A uniform reduction landing inside the promise would suffice, but is not silently substituted for the source’s definition. Under \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\) the two displayed alternatives are disjoint. If \(\mathrm P=\mathrm{NP}\), the first alternative already holds for every finite \(A\), since its ordinary CSP is in NP.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean, under the stated \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\) hypothesis, that the displayed dichotomy holds for every permitted \(A,B\), or that it fails. A negative answer must establish a fixed finite \(A\) and a permitted possibly infinite \(B\) such that no completion is in P and at least one decidable completion is not NP-hard under the stated reductions. A positive answer must cover every infinite restriction with decidable CSP, retaining the completion quantifiers. Proving only the already known finite-restriction case, treating an arbitrary input class that is not \(\operatorname{CSP}(B)\), or disproving a stronger uniform hardness requirement does not settle this question. No additional unproved hypothesis may replace the explicitly stated separation assumption.

source_formulation.text: Under P≠NP, do finite-domain restricted CSPs satisfy a polynomial-time versus NP-hard dichotomy when their restriction structures may be infinite?
source_formulation.caption: Editorial paraphrase of the second question in §10; decidability and the completion-based hardness convention are inherited from §3.

context_blocks.text: Restricted CSPs impose a promise on which input structures must be handled. For example, RCSP(K₃,K₄) asks whether a graph promised to be four-colourable is three-colourable; Kᵣ is the complete loopless graph on r vertices. Unlike a promise CSP, the promise here restricts the input class on both yes and no sides rather than relaxing which assignments count as solutions.

The source proves that a finite restriction B permits a reduction to an ordinary CSP on the exponential structure A^B. Its elements are functions from B to A, with relations defined by preservation along relation tuples of B. If A and B are both finite, this is again a finite structure, so the ordinary finite-domain decision dichotomy applies. Theorem 18 records the resulting restricted dichotomy.

An infinite B can impose familiar global input conditions. For directed graphs, the structure on rational numbers with the strict-order relation admits a homomorphism from exactly the finite acyclic digraphs. Such a restriction remains decidable even though its representing structure is infinite. This illustrates why finite assignment domains do not make the promise finite.

The general question preserves arbitrary decidable homomorphism restrictions. It is separate from the source’s neighbouring conjecture asking for a particular algebraic criterion for tractability. The finite exponential construction does not remain a finite template when B is infinite, so the known finite-restriction reduction alone does not prove the target.

The completion definition is essential: an algorithm must be correct only on the promised class, yet it must halt on every input. Hardness quantifies over every decidable total extension of that promised behaviour. Saying merely that the intersection of two CSP languages is NP-hard would describe one particular extension and would not prove the required universal hardness.
